abstract:
Deduction and static equivalence are central knowledge problems in the formal analysis of security protocols and are known to be undecidable for general equational theories. Several decidable classes have been identified through structural restrictions, including subterm convergent theories, shallow permutative theories, contracting theories and some are implemented in tools such as ProVerif and DeepSec. 
We identify two recurring themes: symbol preservation, where symbols are maintained across axioms, and symbol contraction, where symbols decrease in depth or number from left to right. 
For symbol-preserving systems, we introduce measure-invariant (MI) and separate measure-invariant (SMI) theories, generalizing permutative classes and providing new decidable fragments for deduction and static equivalence. Depth-sensitive refinements, including depth-preserving permutative (DPP) and depth-preserving variable-permuting (DPVP) theories, are case studies to understand whether the depth of occurrences of symbols matter. For symbol-contraction systems, we define depth-decreasing (DD) and variable-preserving function-decreasing (VBFD) theories, capturing some simple relaxations of term contraction; while deduction is undecidable in general, these restrictions highlight potential decidable fragments. 
Overall, our results show that controlling symbol dynamics in rewrite rules provides a unifying perspective on the decidability of knowledge problems, offering conceptual clarity on what makes these problems hard for different equational theories.

 1      Introduction
Knowledge problems, such as deduction (the problem of determining which messages an
intruder can deduce from a given set of messages in a security protocol) and static equival-
ence (the problem of determining whether two set of messages in a security protocol are
distinguishable by the attacker) [2], are central to the formal symbolic analysis of security
protocols because they model what an adversary can learn or compute from interacting with
cryptographic messages. In such a symbolic analysis, the adversary’s capabilities, in terms of
their ability to manipulate cryptographic messages, can be modeled as an equational theory.
The complexity of both problems depends on the underlying equational model of the attacker,
and for some equational theories, they are undecidable. Over the years, researchers have
studied structural restrictions on equational theories that yield decidable classes. Examples

       local finiteness [1]. These results have influenced the development of verification tools, such
       as ProVerif [7], AKiSS [10], DeepSec [12], SPEC [26], APTE [11], and SATEQUIV [15].
           Although these classes have been studied extensively, it was not always clear how the
       decidability results for one class relate to others, and why some restrictions imposed one one
       class of theories restore decidability while others do not. Most existing characterizations
       focus on closure properties, termination arguments, or saturation procedures. While effective,
       these approaches give limited insight into the structural reasons behind decidability or
       undecidability, and extending these results to new equational theories often requires ad
       hoc arguments. This work is a preliminary attempt at providing a unifying framework for
       studying the decidability of the knowledge problems, from a structural perspective based
       on the positions and depths of symbols in term rewriting rules. Our intuition is that the
       decidability of knowledge problems is closely linked to how symbols occur and propagate
       across different depths of terms during rewriting and deduction. By making this behavior
       explicit, we aim to provide a clearer and more intuitive explanation of existing results and to
       offer a framework for studying decidability boundaries in a more systematic and fine-grained
       way. This perspective is not meant to replace existing techniques, but to complement them,
       clarify known results, and guide the search for new decidable classes.


       Related work. A prominent class of equational theories for which the knowledge problems
       are decidable is the class of subterm-convergent theories [1]. In these theories, every term
       on the right-hand side of an equation is a constant or a strict subterm of the left-hand side,
       ensuring that rewriting reduces terms structurally. Beyond subterm-convergent theories, more
       general algebraic structures have been considered to model various properties of cryptographic
       operations. For example, associative-commutative (AC) theories handle operations that are
       ubiquitous in cryptography such as exclusive-or, modular addition, or model situations in
       which the order of performing certain cryptographic operations is irrelevant [16]. Some of
       these algebraic equations, despite appearing simple, require more sophisticated techniques to
       compute deducibility, which is central to symbolic protocol analysis and its automation. In
       fact, certain equations render this problem undecidable [1, 24, 9, 20].
           One line of work extending this result is to identify broad classes of equational theories
       for which deducibility and static equivalence become decidable. Permutative and leaf-
       permutative theories [18], generalizing the AC theories, pursue this direction by allowing
       variables to be permuted across equations, introducing a controlled way of manipulating
       messages while preserving certain structural invariants. On the other hand, graph-embedded
       and homeomorphic-embedding equational theories [24], generalizing the subterm-convergent
       theories, capture various equations that model reductions or contractions on the messages,
       with the possibility of small permutation in the end.
           In this paper, we propose a unifying view of existing work and suggest potential directions
       for understanding the “shape” of decidability by studying the structure of term rewriting rules.
       We also provide results along these directions by analyzing different classes of equational
       theories with respect to the structure and dynamics of symbols in their rewrite rules.
           Based on our review of existing theoretical approaches discussed above, we organise our
       work into two main themes, based on how symbols appear in rewrite rules. The first theme
       covers the cases when both sides of the equations in a theory preserve the symbols, either in
       terms of their number of occurrences (as in permutative theories) or in more restricted forms
       – for example, when the positions of internal symbols on both sides are fixed while variables
       at leaf positions are permuted. The second theme arises when symbols decrease or contract

Summary of contributions. Our contribution is to discuss these two main themes in a more
structured way, by directly analyzing the positions and dynamics of symbols in the axioms
of our equational theories.
    For the first theme, we generalize known results by introducing a class of theories broader
than permutative theories, for which deduction remains decidable. Instead of requiring that
the number of occurrences of every symbol be preserved on both sides of an axiom (as in
permutative theories), we only require the preservation of a measure or sum of weights
of function symbols and constants (or names), while the number of occurrences of each
variable must remain the same on both sides. This is far more relaxed: non-variable symbols
appearing on one side of the equation do not need to appear on the other side, as long
as they remain balanced in some sense (for example, represented by other non-variable
symbols). This class captures many practical equational theories, such as Diffie–Hellman
exponentiation rules and vector component-wise operations. Since static equivalence for this
more general class is undecidable (because it includes permutative theories), we also examine
restrictions of this class. Additionally, we explore alternative ways to restrict permutative
theories by analyzing how the levels (depths) of symbol occurrences on both sides of axioms
affect decidability. We prove some preliminary results, and this ongoing work aims to provide
initial insights into how the positioning of symbols in axioms can influence the decidability
of knowledge problems from a term-rewriting perspective.
    For the second theme, in which the axioms appear to model the extraction of messages,
we describe how this behavior can be captured by depth-decreasing properties of symbols:
each symbol occurs deeper on the left-hand side and shallower on the right-hand side of
an axiom. This provides a more natural and intuitive way of seeing how messages are

       Organization of the paper. Section 2 introduces the technical preliminaries and notation,
       including term algebras, equational theories, term rewriting systems, and the knowledge prob-
       lems of deduction and static equivalence. Section 3 addresses the first theme of structurally
       balanced equational theories. We revisit known results based on symbol preservation, such as
       permutative theories, and study refinements of this theme. We introduce measure-invariant
       (MI) theories, which generalize permutative theories and admit decidable deduction, and
       identify a restricted subclass, separate measure-invariant (SMI) theories, for which static
       equivalence is decidable. We also study depth-based restrictions of permutative theories:
       depth-preserving permutative (DPP) theories, for which static equivalence remains unde-
       cidable, and the more restrictive depth-preserving variable-permuting (DPVP) theories, for
       which we conjecture decidability of static equivalence. The relationship between various
       classes of theories studied under this theme is summarised in the left figure in Figure 1.
           Section 4 focuses on the second theme of structurally decreasing equational theories,
       inspired by subterm-convergent systems. We introduce depth-decreasing (DD) theories and
       show that deduction is undecidable for this class. We then study a restricted subclass,
       variable-balanced function-decreasing (VBFD) theories, which preserves variable occurrences
       while strictly decreasing function symbols, and discuss how this restriction provides insight
       into the role of symbol-position dynamics. The relationship between theories studied under
       this theme is summarised in the right figure in Figure 1.
           Section 5 concludes with a summary of results and directions for future work. Overall,
       the paper provides a structural, symbol-position–based perspective on the decidability of
       knowledge problems in symbolic protocol analysis.

2.2      Equational Theory and Term Rewriting
Let E be a set of pairs of terms (l, r) ∈ T (Σ, X) × T (Σ, X). We write each pair (l, r) ∈ E as
an equation l ≈ r, where l and r are called the left-hand side (lhs) and right-hand side (rhs),
respectively. The equational theory ≈E is defined as the smallest congruence relation on
T (Σ, X) containing all equations l ≈ r ∈ E that is closed under substitutions and contexts.
By abuse of notation, we often refer to E as an equational theory, meaning the induced
relation ≈E .
    An equational theory can be used to abstract and model the computational abilities of
an attacker in interactive cryptographic protocols. A classical example is the Dolev–Yao
model [17], which treats cryptographic operators as black boxes, meaning decryption is only
possible with the correct key and no partial information is leaked.
    A simple instance is the equational theory for symmetric encryption:

     ESEnc = {dec(enc(x, y), y) ≈ x, fst(⟨x, y⟩) ≈ x, snd(⟨x, y⟩) ≈ y}.                                (1)

   In the Dolev–Yao framework, this theory is interpreted over the term algebra T (Σ, V ∪ N ),
where enc, dec, fst, snd, and ⟨·, ·⟩ are function symbols in Σ, variables range over V , and
atomic messages (e.g., nonces and keys) are names in N . The model relies on two main
simplifications. First, names abstract bitstrings and are indivisible. Second, it assumes
perfect cryptography: the only way to recover m from enc(m, k) is by knowing k, i.e., applying
dec(enc(m, k), k) ≈E m.

 3     Structurally Balanced Rewrite Rules
In this section, we review both classical and recent results concerning equations in which the
occurrences of symbols are, in some sense, preserved from left to right. We begin with a review
of the most general classes, the permutative and leaf-permutative classes, in Section 3.1.
The decidability problems for these classes have been extensively studied in [18]. Section 3.2
presents our new contributions in refining the permutative classes.

3.1    Revisiting Permutative TRS
We discuss here some known results on permutative classes and its restrictions. These classes
and their restrictions have been extensively studied not only in the context of knowledge
problems, but also more broadly, for example in connection with unification problems in
term rewriting.

▶ Definition 5 (Permutative [18]). An equation l ≈ r is permutative if for every (function,
variable, name) symbol, its number of occurrences in l is the same as in r. An equational
theory E is permutative if every equation in E is permutative.

▶ Definition 6 (Leaf-Permutative [18]). An equation l ≈ r is is leaf-permutative if r is a leaf
permutation of l, i.e., r = lσ, where σ is a permutation of the leaf nodes of l. An equational
theory E is leaf-permutative if every equation in it is leaf-permutative.

   Note that leaf-permutativity also requires the non-variable leaf nodes to be permuted. In
the following, we focus on a class in which only the occurrences of variables are considered.

▶ Definition 7 (Variable Permuting Equation and Theory [9]). An equation l ≈ r is said to be
variable permuting if all the following conditions are satisfied:
1. the set of occurrences of l is identical to the set of occurrences of r, i.e. pos(l) = pos(r).
2. for any non-variable occurrence p of r, l(p) = r(p),
3. for any x ∈ var(l) ∪ var(r), the number of occurrences of x in l is identical to the number
   of occurrences of x in r.
An equational theory E is a variable-permuting if every equation in it is variable-permuting.

▶ Definition 8 (Shallow Equation and Theory [9]). An equation l ≈ r is shallow if variables
can only occur at a position at depth at most 1 in both l and r. An equational theory E is
shallow if every equation in it is shallow.

▶ Definition 9 (Separate Variable Permuting (SVP) Theory [9]). An equational theory E is said
to be separate variable-permuting (SVP) if E is variable-permuting and for any l = r ∈ E, l
and r are rooted by the same function symbol that does not occur elsewhere in E.

       3.2     Refinement to permutative classes
       We consider several refinements of the class of permutative equational theories and related
       notions. First, we introduce a broader class, called size-invariant equational theories, in which
       equations preserve term size under arbitrary substitutions; deduction remains decidable for
       this class. Second, we define the depth-preserving permutative class, which forms a subclass
       of permutative equational theories and therefore also admits decidable deduction. This
       class intersects with the class of leaf-permutative theories, but neither contains it nor is
       contained in it. Using similar proof techniques, we further show that static equivalence
       remains undecidable for this class.

4.2    Refining the structural decreasing properties
We start with a relaxed notion of depth-decreasing, where at least one symbol in a term
moves to a strictly shallower depth.
    First, existing definitions of contracting term rewriting systems (TRS) are technically
involved and not very transparent. They rely on intricate syntactic constraints that are often
implicit in the reasoning. Although checking whether a TRS is contracting is straightforward,
the notion is not always semantically natural as a characterization of structural decrease. In
particular, graph-embedded TRS may violate arity consistency under syntactic manipulations,
suggesting the need for a more direct symbolic notion of structural reduction.
    Second, many equational theories model operations that extract or manipulate subterms,
as in cryptographic primitives such as encryption, digital signatures, and blind signatures.

resulting term. Symbolically, this corresponds to some symbols moving upward in depth,

ascends. Even if we restrict to transformations where symbols only ascend or stay at the same
depth, this relaxed depth-decreasing notion still captures structural simplification. However,
as we show, even under this seemingly well-behaved restriction, the associated knowledge

 5     Conclusion and future work
In this paper, we take a structural view of the decidability of knowledge problems, focusing
on how symbols are positioned and transformed in term rewriting rules. We identify two
recurring principles – symbol preservation and symbol contraction – and study them via
symbol depth and position dynamics. This perspective explains why closely related classes
may differ in decidability of deduction or static equivalence.
    For symbol preservation, we generalise permutative theories to measure-invariant (MI)
theories, where preservation is relaxed to a weight measure. MI theories admit decidable
deduction and capture practical examples such as Diffie–Hellman exponentiation and vector
operations. We refine this to separate measure-invariant (SMI) theories, for which static equi-
valence is decidable, and further study depth-sensitive variants, including depth-preserving
permutative (DPP) and depth-preserving variable-permuting (DPVP) theories, which isolate
the effect of symbol depth on decidability.
    For symbol contraction, we introduce depth-decreasing (DD) theories to model operations
such as message extraction. While deduction is undecidable in general, the variable-preserving
function-decreasing (VBFD) fragment highlights a meaningful restricted class with better
structural control.
    Overall, our results show that controlling symbol balance and depth provides a principled
way to understand the boundary of decidability in knowledge problems, offering both
conceptual clarity and insight for symbolic protocol analysis.
